title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: John Bailes
summary: John Bailes reflects on how their life has been shaped by various experiences and relationships that have contributed to their understanding of themselves and the world. They share stories about their journey, including being involved in an accident, exploring alternative interests like poetry and philosophy, and meeting influential figures in Buddhism, which ultimately led them to discover Zen Buddhism and find a sense of fulfillment and transformation through their practice. Through these experiences, they have come to understand that their path has been one of opening to love, heart, gratitude, and generosity, and that this experience is always present, but only now is it fully accessible.

sentences.text: Hello everybody.
Thank you for being here.
The shuso talk is called the way-seeking mind talk.
In a sense it's who am I, where did I come from, how did I get here, and what was the burr under my saddle that made me a Buddhist.

So when I think about how I've come to this place, to Bellingham, to the Red Cedar Zen Community and Dharma Hall, to be shuso sharing with you the seeming long and winding trail that's apparently led here, words like blessed, lucky, auspicious, charmed, maverick, grateful, generosity, kindness, humble, humbled, and love come to mind.

What I'm given to believe and say is my practice doesn't seem to be the result of chronology, a series of causal relationships that describe a straight line leading in a clear direction through space from one point to another point, from no practice to practice.
Each point, each moment is a universe, entire, speaking, opening, yielding, giving, giving each of us.
There are no averages, there's only each moment, whether we know we are present or not.
We're each this unique snowflake and we're just as ephemeral.
We don't repeat.
There are no do-overs.
It's not like you have to get it right the first time either, whatever getting it right means.
And yet each moment's an opportunity.
Sometimes sitting zazen, practicing, it's as though our sense of time is sometimes like one moment, 10,000 years.
It could be one moment, 10,000 years of pain, one moment, 10,000 years of joy.
Our lives turn on each of these moments.
When I look back over my life and I try to give some storyline to it, I find it's much more like the movie or novel genre, magical realism, like Bread and Chocolate or fried green tomatoes.
I can't remember the patron saint, the woman in Mexico, the lady who's on all the handbags and t-shirts, Guadalupe.
She appears, boom, in the middle of tomatoes, in the middle of preparing lunch, the Tenzo.
So in many ways and in one way, traveling this path is truly a journey without a goal.
The path itself is all there is.
Most of us spend a long time looking for the path.
For me, it seems a long opening to love, heart.
And when I say heart, I actually mean my understanding and my experience of this Chinese and Japanese word shin, which has, I think, been translated heart mind.
So not separating the intellect and the emotions, and not, when I say heart, only meaning emotions.
So for me, it seems like a long opening to love, heart, gratitude, and generosity.
It's as though this experience has always been here, only that I open to it.
When I open, when I open, everything and everyone is with me forever, now, a moment.

When I look back from this place and [unclear: "write the past"], I'm nothing but a long line of other people: friends, enemies, lovers, family, history, culture, artists, all of whom have given me parts of me.
Each has passed to me their light, their hope, their bodhicitta.
Each seems forever with me, presences in my being right here.
And this includes you, that you are here.
I am.

I have a birth certificate that says I was born to Maria Lakava Bales and Edgar Hackney Bales at 2:45 in the morning, Eastern Standard Time, on April 11th, 1952, in Jamaica Hospital, Jamaica, Queens, New York.
And that I am John Edgar Bales, present.
Thus it is said.
It seems I knew little of what I was stepping into, the meeting of my father's and mother's karma in me, and whatever I brought with me to the show.
An only child born to a 42 year old man and a 33 year old woman, I was loved and wanted and thus lived happily ever after.
Well, not exactly.

At my home, my home now in Boston with my wife Jessa, we have a photograph of me as a one or a two year old sitting on my butt with my legs extended straight out, torso straight and this sort of big smile on my face, just looking out.
It's done from a couple of different angles.
It may be one of these photographs like this, yeah, and it has like four different little shots in circles.
With my legs extended, the remarkable thing about this is it looks pretty much like I do now.
I don't know if it's remarkable, but of course my beard is not white and I don't have a beard and there is actually some hair on top of my head.
I think it was toe head.
But there's no mistaking this person.
It's me and I was it.
The energy, the eyes, it's really sort of remarkable.
It's one of those pictures I had sitting away somewhere in a file some day and your spouse finds it and they go, well, we've got to put this up.
So my wife looks at the picture and she goes, that's John, and friends look at that picture and they say the same thing, that's John.
And each of us has these photos and it's not particularly extraordinary and still it's amazing.
I'm amazed.
Where did this guy come from?
How does this guy relate to that guy?
How does that guy relate to this guy?
What is that?
But I reached about 13, and that's where the next paragraph sort of starts, maybe 14.

So much of my life has been about denying or rejecting or not opening to this John that's given, as though I were not it, or more accurately, my perception of it was too limiting, like a prison of identity to which I would be bound to conform, as though I were a screen onto which people were projecting their image of me and that the expectations to conform to that image, that role, were my death now.
I sensed that very clearly, reasonably early.
But growing up, I grew up on Long Island in New York, about 50 or 60 miles east of New York on what's called the South Shore on a tidal estuary called the Great South Bay.
Growing up here in the 50s and 60s was in many ways wonderful.
It hadn't yet been overrun by cars and housing developments, shopping centers, warehouses and factories.
There was a lot of wildlife, a lot of fowl, a number of farms and clamming, mussels, crabs.
So there are fish and clams and mussels and tidal estuaries, inlets, barrier beaches, the Atlantic Ocean, tomatoes, squash, autumn, winter.
There were creeks and lakes and forts and gunfights and creek mud.
Annie Oakley's Bar X Ranch, whoever made that up, Frankenstein's Shack in the Woods.
All sorts of mystery.
Playing doctor on Dorothy Corton's porch, frogs, lizards, fish.

One example: I remember this idyllic moment when my father had about a 30 some odd foot power boat that we would use for fishing and outings in the bay and sometimes out in the ocean and around Long Island.
After a day out on our boat, my father, mother and I would be coming into the marina and we would be going in a sort of east northeasterly direction coming across the bay from the inlet.
My father would be at the helm on what's called the port side, left side looking forward, standing, and my mother would be standing on the starboard side looking forward.
Both of them would be looking forward, and I would be behind them a little bit, about five feet, sitting on the engine box looking backwards, looking at the stern as the sun was setting.
And my parents are looking forward and the boat is powering along just humming and I'm sitting on the engine box humming and the sun setting.
And the sun is setting and the light from the sun is coming right down to the water to the stern of the boat.
And I'm just totally happy and like just calm and it's as though you could walk from that boat right up to the sun.
All was right in the universe.
It was one of those moments right out of Carl Jung or something, the archetypes.
Soon though, this secure world was broken.
My father was diagnosed with cancer and died within a year, a month before my 11th birthday.
Chaos and confusion seemed to come crashing through, tossing our life, my mother's and mine, up into the air and upside down.
My father was a pretty active man.
He ran a small construction company, loved to work outdoors, could weld, take care of things, do the work he needed to do and hire people to work, but he was somewhat independent.
He loved to garden as well and I loved to garden with him.
I'd become very attached.
It was like even when he'd walk out the front door to, say, move the car from the driveway to the garage, I'd say, Daddy, can I come along?
Used to irritate him sometimes, but he died of a cancer of the thyroid gland in 1963, which is something generally people don't die of today.
And it may be that they just caught it too late, but he also underwent this sort of ridiculous treatment, somewhat more barbaric than even they do with cancer patients now: cobalt.
So they burned his tumor in his neck with cobalt, I guess it's radiation treatment.
And my father went from someone who was like a healthy, vigorous man of 6'2", 210 pounds, active and so on, to someone who basically shriveled up to be about 113 pounds.
One of the most poignant experiences in my youth was one day I was mouthing off to my mother when my father was ill, and he turned around and slapped me across the face.
And I knew something was up because I didn't feel it.
And I remember starting to cry because I didn't feel it more than it hurt.
Then one day I was coming home from school, getting off the bus, and I looked up the street and saw our doctor's car backing very fast out of our driveway and then zooming down the street.
And as the car went by, I remember looking in the car, this is one of these moments, 10,000 years type things.
I remember seeing the doctor, he was very upset and he was crying.
And I knew, but I didn't articulate.
And I went home and my mother came to the door and sent me next door to be with a neighbor, Mrs.
Kramer, who took care of me.
It was definitely a key point in my life.
At any rate, one of the great gifts my father gave me amongst many before he died is that he tutored me at home after school in the evenings for two years, so sort of like fourth and fifth grade.
He didn't feel that I was learning what I should be learning in the public school.
And although he went to private schools, he didn't want me to go to private schools for some reason.

So the remarkable thing is, he started tutoring me and he taught me math, this is by the time I'm in fifth grade, through algebra, and writing skills and science and various things, all from regular books.
But unwittingly, he set me up for a career of cruising through school.
The cruising didn't really strike till about eighth grade, four years later, when finally the anger erupted.
And I began to realize there seemed to be a disconnect between who my mother, teachers and coaches, basically adults, thought I was or wanted me to be.
And not so much, I say here, who I thought I was, but it wasn't so much who I thought it was, it was more like what I didn't know and what it seemed they didn't know.
And that nobody ever talked about what we didn't know.
Nobody ever, ever, it was always too uneasy.
One example would be, I was smart enough to be, I guess, in honor society and a couple of things like that and have some athletic trophies.
And I remember one day having an argument with my mother, or just being a jerk, not really having an argument with my mother.
And I grabbed this plaque you get from the honor society, threw it on the floor, started jumping up and down on it saying, this is not me.
So no one seemed to want to address the missing in my life or our life.
And so there seemed to be some rupture.
And the more I looked at this, the more I found other kids in the same circumstances.
Alcohol, drugs, promiscuity were not far away.
And with school and athletics on cruise control, I was able to maintain what I experienced as a sort of alter life.
I referred to it when I spoke in Vancouver as sort of the local demi-mond.
There are just, a whole group of us who were single-parent children, or children of parents who were having affairs or were alcoholics or whatever.
We would hang together and commiserate, basically, and explore something beyond.
I wouldn't say it was explore.
It wasn't like we were.
It was like we knew we lived in this world that was through the looking glass.
It was clear.
So it led me in many ways, other than the list of things, alcohol, drugs and promiscuity type stuff.
I was also into reading, and I would read poetry and Allen Ginsberg and Bertrand Russell, Hermann Hesse and Sartre and various other people.
In some weird way, I understood that the two different worlds couldn't talk to one another.
I also realized that I was pretty lucky, because I could get really good grades and I could do well in athletics.
I saw that as my ticket out of my hometown, basically.
I didn't have to study very much.
So I had these two worlds going on.
One identity was the good student and athlete, and that was going to get me out of town.
The other, had I acted on it too much, would probably have condemned me to some life in proximity to my hometown, which is not where I wanted to be.
I did have some friends who ended up in a second-floor walk-up over a retail store on Main Street and Bayshore without too many prospects there.
The remarkable thing is that I actually survived.
And that's it.
One of the best things that actually happened to me is that I got out of town and went to a good college that I was accepted into.
I was finally far enough away from home, far enough away from the old sort of John, to make a choice.
I chose not to continue with sports, and I chose to explore philosophy and poetry and so on.
I had some very good luck.

I somehow stumbled into a course on Chinese history and culture and found myself shortly thereafter reading things like the Diamond Sutra and the Lankavatara Sutra and studying the poetry of Sutongpo and various people like this of Tang and Song Dynasty China.
I remember reading the Diamond Sutra and I said, these people actually, I mean, they're talking like I think I'm seeing the world.
These are the first people I've ever run into who seem to make sense to me.
I've got to find out who they are.
Then there was one other instance that actually catapulted me out, that allowed me to say, okay, I'm going to go follow this.
I have to follow this.
I actually have no choice.
I'd gone through this work of putting together an independent concentration, because I couldn't fit what I wanted to do into what existed.
It included Buddhism and various other elements across a number of concentrations.
Where I was, you had to put the whole thing together.
You had to get your three years of tutors, and get your senior tutor lined up for your thesis, and then submit this to the board or something or other.
They look at it, and hopefully the senior tutor you've set things up with will speak for you as well, and you go on.
So I got that all set up, and it took a while, and then I sort of realized, God, I may have to be an academic.
I wasn't sure that I could commit to that.
I wasn't particularly impressed with the academics, as far as what I perceived as the quality of their lives and their relationship with the world.
Then I was visiting a friend in Vermont and I was driving home and I totaled a car.
It was quite a remarkable experience.
I was driving home from Middlebury, Vermont, heading for Long Island, and I was crossing the Hudson River on this small bridge.
I was driving a little MG.
It was early in the morning, and I came around a curve and there was a lip right at the edge of the bridge.
It was a metal grate bridge, and it bumped up the back end of the car as I hit the bridge.
The tires came down, and it was an old bridge and the grates were wide enough to actually catch the wheels, the tires of this car.
Then I remember sitting in this car doing 360s, careening from one side to the other side, and the sky, the river, different things going by.
Then I look up and this person is entering the bridge from the other side in a car, and luckily the passenger side of my car went slamming into his front end.
I remember jumping out of my car and running over to see that this person was okay.
Remarkably enough, I didn't even have a bruise on me.
But being a kid of those days, I had no identification on me.
At that time I worked for a state park, and we had these sort of skivvies, I don't know what you'd call them, some type of uniform but not quite a uniform.
It looked more like a prison outfit, a sort of gray, dingy cotton thing, and I was heading to work directly, so I figured I'd put it on and get there.
At any rate, this is 400 miles from home.
I was compartmentalist long enough that a state trooper arrived, and I was able to tell him who I was and what my phone number was, and then I passed out.
I woke up in a hospital a couple of days later.
After having this very serene sort of experience, I actually left my body from the hospital bed and rose above the bed and was sort of in the corner by the ceiling in the wall there.
I was watching the doctors come and go and the nurses and so on, and then all of a sudden I woke up and my mother was at the foot of the bed.
This is just what a mother loves to hear: I go, what are you doing here?
Get the picture why I don't have children.
But I had this experience, and it was like, God, everything is really okay.
It doesn't matter.
I'd been doing TM prior to that, and I'd been having these experiences in TM where I would almost feel as though you could put my hand through me or something.
Or if I got up too soon after meditation, I think I could walk through the door.
At any rate, I had this experience, and I remember driving home, and my mother obviously was upset.
I remember saying to her, don't worry.
Then I used this dumb phrase like, it doesn't matter.
Everything is okay.
She didn't particularly buy into that.
But something happened.
When I went back to school that next semester, it became very clear to me.
The interesting thing too is that I also found out that I stopped doing TM, because I had the proclivity to sort of take off, and started sitting Zen, where you don't go anywhere.
It took a long time.
Then I trundled out.
This is February 1972, the second semester of my sophomore year, starting.
I called my mom up and said, I'm taking a leave of absence.
That's just what your mom wants to hear.
She didn't go to college.
She grew up in Brooklyn, the youngest daughter of eight children of an Italian immigrant, brought up mostly by her stepsister or half-sister.
Apparently his father had a number of wives who had died.
Things like the flu and all that stuff were pretty nasty then.
At any rate, she didn't particularly appreciate that, and I couldn't particularly understand it.
I didn't exactly have the emotional space to be able to explain it to her.
In any way, it's all reaction, at least in the conversation with my mom.
So I went out to the Zen Center, hitchhiked out, checked it out.
Then I did this thing where I said, yeah, this is where I want to be.
Actually, I left thinking I might go to Japan, but then I met these people who sent me here, and I went there.
Then I met people at the Zen Center in San Francisco, and yeah, this works and so on.
So I went back home and told my mom what I was going to do.
Before I left home, we took a trip together around the United States.
She'd never been beyond Pennsylvania.

So here I am, this 19-year-old guy with actually a beard and long hair, driving around the country with his mom in a Pontiac Catalina, staying in Holiday Inns and what have you, and having a reasonably good time, being not as difficult as I might have been, I think.
We got as far as San Francisco, and I showed her the Zen Center.
Then we took a trip down to Tassajara, and I showed her Tassajara, because I wanted her to know that I wasn't going off to Guyana.
I didn't know that yet, but go off to Guyana to take Kool-Aid or whatever.
This really made sense considering what I was studying, and these people are okay, and the stuff that happens here isn't so bad.
Then we drove home, the northern route, whatever.
Then I came back and took up residence at the Zen Center operation.
My first job there, I worked at Kirby's Ice Cream Parlor, which is at the corner of Laguna between Fell and Oak, I think, where the old expressway used to come down.
That neighborhood is known for its poverty, prostitution, male and female, drugs, and so on and so forth.
I would work at this little ice cream joint making banana walnut ice cream or whatever and serving it.
We would close at midnight.
Somewhere after 10 o'clock at night, the heroin addicts and the transvestites, [unclear: "prostressors"] and prostitutes would show up looking for their sweet fixes, with runny noses and so on.
Also across the street, there was this wonderful blues bar that was frequented by black people in their 1970s clothes, like what you see in those movies.
I remember going to that place one night, or two nights actually, with a woman named Peggy Regue.
Peggy was also a young Zen student who left to become a lawyer, went to Berkeley.
So there we were.
Then slowly I got more entrenched and more involved in the Zen Center.
But my aim basically was to go there to study, to find a job that would support me and pay my rent so I could work four or five hours a day and sit zazen and basically study Buddhism.
I did that.
Then I shipped off to Tassajara for three years, and then came back and was involved at Green Gulch for a little while, and was ordained.
Richard Baker was my teacher.
I had some incredible contact with him.
Richard was the first person that I really met who I felt I could talk to.
One important thing in Buddhism, I think, is being with a teacher you can talk to, whether what you're saying means anything or not.
But if you have the experience that you're able to say things, are you expressing yourself?
This is good.
The only way that a teacher can help us is for us to speak, to reveal ourselves to them as we reveal ourselves to ourselves.
It's easily a two-way street.
We have to put that energy forth, and to find someone that you can work with that allows that to occur is really great.
I was fortuitous enough that I met Richard and we worked together, and I felt very close with him for many years.
He was able to hook me up with my next mentor, who was a woman on the East Coast by the name of Nancy Wilson Ross.
Nancy is dead now.
She died in 19, I want to say, 87.
She was born in 1904.
She comes from more or less this neck of the woods.
I think she grew up somewhere down near Olympia.
Her family came, what was her family's name?
I may remember it, but they came from New England to the northwest in the mid-19th century and were involved with lumber or something.
She went to the University of Oregon and graduated from there in 1920-something or other.
She was a bright woman.
Amongst her incredible history, she was involved in Buddhism in New York way back in the 30s with a Zen teacher, Sokayang, I think his name was.
The first Zen Institute of America grew up from his work, and a woman named Mary Farkas established it.
Nancy was deeply involved and central in helping to get Buddhism established in western, I'll say rich people's culture, so to speak.
She was on the board of the Japan Society and the Asia Society and wrote a number of books.
She was incredibly well-connected and helped the Zen world of the 70s make connections with people who had money to support it.
So the Johnsons of fidelity world, John Rockefeller and Lawrence Rockefeller, and remember the Chester Carlson of Xerox.
These are all people who gave millions of dollars to establish Buddhism in America in the 70s and 80s, and they were very friendly.
They helped the Zen Center and they helped other Zen Centers.
They helped, I guess, Edo Roshi as well.
And I was lucky enough to be involved with Nancy.
I helped her write her last book, which I think is called Buddhism, A Way of Life and Thought.
As she said, this book, she would say to me and a number of us, is for your parents so that they can get some sense of what you're doing and how you're doing it.
It wasn't meant to be necessarily a Dharma book, but a book that could familiarize people with the culture it came from, and the stories about how it was organized.

When I came back to the Zen Center from Nancy's, I'd spent pretty much, off and on, three years there in New York City, Upper East Side type stuff and the North Shore of Long Island, and met incredible, remarkable people.
I remember one day riding in a taxi from some party, and I'm this 25 year old kid from a place called West Islip that is basically a block of split levels.
And I'm in a taxi cab driving north, uptown from Greenwich Village, with Franz Klein's wife.
Just amazing things.
And getting a private tour from Blanchette Rockefeller of the Museum of Modern Art Cezanne show.
It's like magic in some funny way.
At any rate, when I came back to the Zen Center, I became Dick's assistant.
So I was twenty-four seven with him and worked hard and did things.
At a certain point, Dick and I, it was about 1983, and this is another aspect of how you relate with your teacher, I couldn't talk with him anymore.
My experience was that he was blocking me in my practice.
Certain situations were happening where it didn't feel helpful to me.
I'd been at the Zen Center from 19 to 32 or so, I guess, 32, this 32 year.
I thought I wanted to go off and return to the university, finish up there and see what the world was about in some way.
Dick didn't particularly like that idea, but that wasn't what happened, really.
Then, of course, the events of 1983-84 unfolded.
At that time, I was the Eno at the city center, and so I decided to stay another year to help, if I could, stabilize things.
I did.
And then I felt very strongly that, hey, wow, it's not working with Dick anymore.
And there were a number of people just senior to me who, at the time it looked to me, were going to take control of the Zen Center, if you will.
I didn't feel as though I could mature there, and I felt I needed to be someplace else to learn and study.
So I left.
I went back to the university and I got some degrees.
Then I went into business to pay off my debts, and I built a division of a regional financial planning firm from nothing to a relatively good size business.
At a certain point, after doing that, I'm very good at zeroing in on something and then focusing on it and getting it done.
That's where "maverick," the term, comes in.
So I did that, and it was really great.
I was totally engrossed in it and made this thing happen.
Then one day I woke up and I said, I'm in management.
And I'm really a nice guy, but I have a really hard time managing to what I call the status quo.
I'm much better at starting things up and making things go and then getting the next thing going.
So my partners agreed.
I went back more into personal practice and at the same time fell in love with sailing.
And then, I'm dangerous.
I fall in love with these things.
The next thing I knew, I was applying to be in a sailboat race around the world, and the next thing I knew, I was accepted.
The next thing I knew, I was studying weather and navigation.
I was the navigator and tactician on this team race around the world with 12 identical one design yachts in 2000, 2001.
I did that, and I came back and it was like, God, I can't be in an office.
I'd been outside so much, and it was so wondrous.
The idea of being in one of those offices, not the experience, my skin crawled.
But yeah, God, there's so many stories to tell.
I can't tell you what it's like being out in the southern ocean.
Or I can, I'll tell you this little bit.
The air temperature is 32 degrees, the water temperature is 32 degrees, the wind's blowing 50 or 60 knots, and the seas are 50 feet high.
And it's pitch black.
And you're wet.
We only have two people on deck, one person manning the main sheet on the big mainsail to let it go in case big winds hit, and one person helming.
I was one of the helming people.
The main sheet person could only stay on deck for 15 minute stints and the helms person could only helm for 30 minutes at a time, and then we'd switch.
From here to where Karen is would be the main sheet person, and I'd be on the helm, and I could shout at the top of my lungs.
She wouldn't hear me.
However, you're dead dog tired, and you know you're going to get awful wet, despite all this high tech clothing we had, and you don't necessarily want to go out there.
So you feel like that sometimes.
But you do.
And then what happens is the southern lights appear, and the sky starts filling in with this great beige and amber light that's crawling up the sides of the horizon and wiggling.
Then it forms this dome over you, and there's green and blue and red in it.
And it's going shh.
You feel like you're in this incredible cathedral.
You forget you're freezing to death and soaking wet.
And it's easy.
You can't see anything, and there are icebergs out there.
And then there are these things called Magellanic clouds, which for all intents and premises appear in the sky in the dark of the night like a white cumulus cloud.
What they are is this cloud of negatively charged ions that are just swelling and going.
It's amazing.
So anyway, I got back from this trip and I became a professional sailboat captain.
I would train people to sail boats in the ocean and sail boats from New England to the Caribbean, Caribbean to New England, across the ocean and back.

Despite all this wonderful stuff, one day a friend of mine, whom I was ordained with, I think we were ordained in 1977, and David is a teacher in the Shambhala lineage now, 2003 I think it was, David called me up in November and said, John, I'm going to be in town for five days.
Can I stay with you?
David and I had remained friends since we were kids.
We both arrived at the Zen Center when we were 19.
We both were out there at Green Gulch breaking clods of clay with rakes and so on as volunteer labor.
He came and visited, and we had a good time and great conversations.
Then I took him up to Karma Choling in northern Vermont, where he had a big meeting, and I met some wonderful people.
I came back home and he had his meeting, and then he went back to Germany.
About three weeks later, he called me up and said, John, I'm leading a program called Sutrayana Seminary at Dechen Choling in France.
It's a 30-day program.
Do you want to come?
I said, sure, not even thinking, or thinking, but not hesitating.
And I went and I had this incredible experience.

The Sutrayana Seminary is about studying the one book we're reading, the Bhikkhu Bodhi stuff, what's called the Hinayana from the Mahayana view, and also the Mahayana through what's called Madhyamaka, Nagarjuna, Vimalakirti, and so on, and the foundations for what's considered the Vajrayana path.
While I was sitting there doing this practice with these people, it was like I had never left.
It was in me: sitting, talking, walking, listening to the practice, reading.
I understood incredible amounts of things that I didn't particularly understand.
Not that I didn't understand before.
I don't understand exactly how to say it, but they made sense in a way that it wasn't like these big things going on.
It was just, oh, this is the way things are.
It's not even like you have to do something, but you have to do something to share it.
So I said, yeah, I have to do something to share it.
I got home and I called Norman, and he said, yeah, well, I'm going to be in Massachusetts on such and such.
I said, okay, let's get together.
We got together, and the next thing you know, we're almost over, or at least we're almost up to now.
The next thing you know, I'm at a sesshin at Loon Lake, raining and cold, much like, well, not as much later as there is now.
I enjoyed it and had a great time and loved the people there.
And the next thing I know, I'm at Samish Island, or actually I'm with Norman in Mexico somewhere.
Then I'm at Samish Island, and someplace along the line, we agree that I ought to be shuso.
My practice, I seem to recognize in 2003, was not about me but about being with other people, and we ought to recognize that together somehow.
So Norman and I hooked up, so to speak.

I'm shuso and participating in the transmission process and learning how to become a Buddhist teacher, for which I'm very grateful to all of you for having me, and to Norman for making it possible, and to all these people in my past for making it possible.
So let's end with thank you.
Great, thank you.

verbatim.text: Hello everybody. Thank you for being here. The shuso talk is called the way-seeking mind talk. In a sense it's who am I, where did I come from, how did I get here, and what was the burr under my saddle that made me a Buddhist. So when I think about how I've come to this place, to Bellingham, to the Red Cedar Zen Community and Dharma Hall, to be shuso sharing with you the seeming long and winding trail that's apparently led here. Words like blessed, lucky, auspicious, charmed, maverick, grateful, generosity, kindness, humble, humbled, and love come to mind. What I'm given to believe and say is my practice doesn't seem to be the result of chronology, a series of causal relationships that describe a straight line

leading in a clear direction through space from one point to another point, from no practice to practice. Each point, each moment is a universe, entire speaking, opening, yielding, giving, giving each of us. There are no averages, there's only each moment whether we know we are present or not. We're each this unique snowflake and we're just as ephemeral. We don't repeat. There are no do-overs. It's not like you have to get it right the first time either, whatever getting it right means. And yet each moment's an opportunity. Sometimes sitting zazen, practicing, it's as though our sense of time is sometimes it's like one moment 10,000 years. It could be one moment 10,000 years of pain,

one moment 10,000 years of joy. Our lives turn on each of these moments. When I look back over my life and I try to give some storyline to it, I find it's much more like the movie or novel genre, magical realism, like bread for chocolate or fried green tomatoes. I can't remember the patron saint, the woman in Mexico, the lady who's on all the handbags and t-shirts, Guadalupe, you know. She appears, boom, in the middle of tomatoes, in the middle of preparing lunch, the Tenzo. So in many ways and in one way, traveling this path is truly a journey without a goal. The path itself is all there is. Most of us spend a long time looking for the path. For me, it seems a long opening to love,

heart. And when I say heart, I actually mean my understanding and my experience of this Chinese and Japanese word shin, which has, I think, been translated heart mind. So not separating the intellect and the emotions, and not when I say heart only meaning emotions. So for me, it seems like a long opening to love, heart, gratitude, and generosity. It's as though this experience has always been here, only that I open to it. When I open, when I open, everything and everyone is with me forever, now a moment. When I look back from this place and write the past, I'm nothing but a long line of other people, friends, enemies, lovers, family, history, culture, artists, all of whom have given me parts of me.

Each has passed to me their light, their hope, their bodhicitta. Each seems forever with me, presences in my being right here. And this includes you, that you are here. I am. I have a birth certificate that says I was born to Maria Lakava Bales and Edgar Hackney Bales at 2.45 in the morning Eastern Standard Time on April 11th, 1952. In Jamaica Hospital, Jamaica, Queens, New York. And that I am John Edgar Bales, present. Thus it is said. It seems I knew little of what I was stepping into, the meeting of my father's and mother's karma in me, and whatever I brought with me to the show. An only child born to a 42 year old man and a 33 year old woman. I was loved and wanted and thus lived happily ever after.

Well, not exactly. At my home, my home now in Boston with my wife Jessa, we have a photograph of me as a one or a two year old sitting on my butt with my legs extended straight out, torso straight and this sort of big smile on my face just looking out. It's done from a couple of different angles. It may be one of these photographs like this, yeah, and it has like four different little shots in circles. With my legs extended and the remarkable thing about this is it looks pretty much like I do now. I don't know if it's remarkable, but of course my beard is not white and I don't have a beard and there is actually some hair on top of my head. I think it was toe head.

But there's no mistaking this person. It's me and I was it. The energy, the eyes, it's really sort of remarkable. It's one of those pictures, you know, I had sitting away somewhere in a file some day and your spouse finds it and they go, well, we've got to put this up. So my wife looks at the picture and she goes, that's John and friends look at that picture and they say the same thing, that's John. And each of us has these photos and it's not particularly extraordinary and still it's amazing. I'm amazed. Where did this guy come from? How does this guy relate to that guy? How does that guy relate to this guy? What is that?

But, you know, I guess I reached about 13 and that's where the next paragraph sort of starts, maybe 14. So much of my life has been about denying or rejecting or not opening to this John that's given as though I were not it or more accurately it was too, my perception of it was too limiting, like a prison of identity to which I would be bound to conform, as though I were a screen onto which people were projecting their image of me and that the expectations to conform to that image, that role, were my death now. I sensed that very clearly, reasonably early. But, you know, growing up, I grew up on Long Island in New York, about 50 or 60 miles east of New York on what's called the South Shore

on a tidal estuary called the Great South Bay. And growing up here in the 50s and 60s was in many ways wonderful. It hadn't yet been overrun by cars and housing developments, shopping centers, warehouses and factories. There were a lot of, there was a lot of wildlife, a lot of fowl, a lot of a number of farms and clamming, mussels, crabs. So, you know, there are fish and clams and mussels and tidal estuaries, inlets, barrier beaches, the Atlantic Ocean, tomatoes, squash, autumn, winter. There were creeks and lakes and forts and gunfights and creek mud. Annie Oakley's Bar X Ranch, whoever made that up, I, you know, Frankenstein's Shack in the Woods. All sorts of mystery. Playing doctor on Dorothy Corton's porch, frogs, lizards, fish.

One example, I remember this idyllic moment when my father had a about a 30 some odd foot power boat that we would use for fishing and outings in the bay and sometimes out in the ocean and around Long Island. When after a day out on our boat, my father, mother and I would be coming into the marina and we would go, be going in a sort of east northeasterly direction coming across the bay from the inlet. And my father would be at the helm on what's called the port side, left side looking forward, standing, and my mother would be standing on the starboard side looking forward. And both of them would be looking forward and would be, and I would be behind them

a little bit about five feet sitting on the engine box looking backwards, looking at the stern as the sun was setting. And my parents are looking forward and the boat is powering along just humming and I'm sitting on the engine box humming and the sun setting. And the sun is setting and the light from the sun is coming right down to the water to the stern of the boat. And I'm just totally happy and like just calm and it's as though you could walk from that boat right up to the sun. All was right in the universe. It was one of those moments right out of Carl Jung or something, you know, the archetypes. Soon though, this secure world was broken. My father was diagnosed with cancer and died within

a year, a month before my 11th birthday. Chaos and confusion seemed to come crashing through tossing our life, my mother's and mine, up into the air and upside down. My father was a pretty active, he ran a small construction company, loved to work outdoors, you know, could weld, take care of things, do his own, do the work he needed to do and hire people to work, but he was somewhat independent. Loved to garden as well and I loved to garden with him. I'd become very attached. It was like even when he'd walk out the front door to say move the car from the driveway to the garage, I'd say, Daddy, can I come along? Used to irritate him sometimes, but he died of a cancer of the

thyroid gland in 1963, which is something generally people don't die of today. And it may be that they just caught it too late, but he also underwent this sort of ridiculous treatment, somewhat more barbaric than even they do with cancer patients now, cobalt. So they burned his tumor in his neck with cobalt, I guess it's radiation treatment. And my father went from someone who was like a healthy, vigorous man of 6'2", 210 pounds, active and so on, to someone who basically shriveled up to be about 113 pounds. One of the most poignant experiences in my youth was one day I was mouthing off to my mother when my father was ill. And he turned around and slapped me across the face.

And I knew something was up because I didn't feel it. And I remember starting to cry because I didn't feel it more than it hurt. Then one day I was coming home from school getting off the bus and I looked up the street and saw our doctor's car backing very fast out of our driveway and then zooming down the street. And as the car went by, I remember looking in the car, this is one of these moments is 10,000 years type things. I remember seeing the doctor, he was very upset and he was crying. And I knew, but I didn't articulate. And I went home and my mother came to the door and sent me next door to be with a neighbor, Mrs. Kramer, who took care of me. It was definitely a key point in my life. At any rate,

my father, one of the great gifts my father gave me amongst many before he died is that he tutored me at home after school in the evenings for two years, so sort of like fourth and fifth grade. And he didn't feel that I was learning what I should be learning in the public school. And although he went to private schools, he didn't want me to go to private schools for some reason. So the remarkable thing is, so he started tutoring me and he taught me math, this is by the time I'm in fifth grade, through algebra and writing skills and science and various things, all from regular books and learned to do math type things. But unwittingly, he set me up for a career of cruising through school. The cruising didn't

really strike till about eighth grade when, you know, four years later, finally the anger erupted. And I began to realize there seemed to be a disconnect between who my mother, teachers and coaches, basically adults, thought I was or wanted me to be. And not so much, I say here who I thought I was, but it wasn't so much who I thought it was, it was more like what I didn't know and what it seemed they didn't know. And that nobody ever talked about what we didn't know. Nobody ever, ever, it was always too uneasy. A couple of simple or one example would be, you know, I was smart enough to be, I guess, to be in honor society and a couple of things like that and have some athletic trophies.

And I remember one day having an argument with my mother or just being a jerk, not really having an argument with my mother. And I grabbed this plaque you get from the honor society, threw it on the floor, started jumping up and down on it saying, this is not me. So no one seemed to want to address the missing in my life or our life. And so there seemed to be some rupture. And the more I looked at this, the more I found other kids in the same circumstances, alcohol, drugs, promiscuity, we're not far away. And with school and athletics on cruise control, I was sort of able to maintain what I experienced as a sort of altar life. I referred to it when I spoke in Vancouver as sort of the local demi-mond. There are just, you know,

a whole group of us who were single parent children or children of parents who are having affairs or alcoholics or whatever. And we would hang together and commiserate basically and explore something beyond. I wouldn't say it was explore. It wasn't like we were, it was like we knew we lived in this world that was through the looking glass. It was clear. So it led me in many ways, other than the list of things, you know, alcohol, drugs and promiscuity type stuff. I also was into reading and I would read poetry and Allen Ginsberg and Bertrand Russell, Herman Hess and Sartre and various other people. In some weird way, I understood that the two different worlds couldn't talk to one another.

And I also realized that I was pretty lucky because I could get really good grades and I could do well in athletics. And I saw that as my ticket out of my hometown, basically. I didn't have to study very much. And so I had these two worlds going on. One identity was the good student and athlete, again, how that was going to get me out of town. And then the other, had I acted on it too much, would probably condemn me to some life in proximity to my hometown, which is not where I wanted to be. You know, I did have some friends who ended up in a second floor walk up over a retail store on Main Street and Bayshore without too many prospects. There. The remarkable thing is that I actually survived. And that's it. Good, two, three.

Yeah, okay. And one of the best things that actually happened to me is I got out of town and went to a good college that I was accepted into. And I was finally at a point that I was far enough that I could make a choice far away from home, far enough away from home in the old sort of John to make a choice. And I chose not to continue with sports and I chose to explore philosophy and poetry and so on. And I had some very good luck. I somehow stumbled into a course on Chinese history and culture and found myself shortly thereafter reading things like the Diamond Sutra and the Lankavatara Sutra and studying the poetry of Sutongpo and various people like this of Tang and Song Dynasty China. And I remember reading the Diamond Sutra and I said,

these people actually, I mean, they're talking like I think I'm seeing the world. These are the first people I've ever run into who seem to make sense to me. I've got to find out who they are. Then there was one other instance that actually catapulted me out that allowed me to say, okay, I'm going to go follow this. I have to follow this. I actually have no choice. I'd gone through this work of putting together an independent concentration because I couldn't fit what I wanted to do in what existed that included Buddhism and various other elements across a number of concentrations. And where I was, you had to put the whole thing together. You had to get your three years of tutors and you

get your senior tutor lined up for your thesis and then submit this to the board or something or other and they look at it and hopefully the senior tutor that you've set things up will speak for you as well and you go on. So I got that all set up and it took a while and then I sort of realized, God, I may have to be an academic. And I wasn't sure that I could commit to that. And I wasn't particularly impressed with the academics as far as what I perceived as the quality of their lives and their relationship with the world. Then I was visiting a friend in Vermont and I was driving home and I totaled a car. It was quite a remarkable experience. I was driving home from Middlebury, Vermont heading

for Long Island and I was crossing the Hudson River on this small bridge and I was driving a little MG. It was early in the morning and I came around a curve and there was a lip right at the edge of the bridge and it was a metal grate bridge and it bumped up the back end of the car as I hit the bridge and the tires came down and it was an old bridge and the grates were wide enough to actually catch the wheels, the tires of this car. So then I remember sitting in this car doing 360s careening from one side to the other side as I'm going the sky, the river, you know, different things. And then I look up and this person is entering this bridge from the other side in the car and luckily the passenger side of my car went slamming into his

front end. And I remember jumping out of my car and running over to see that this person was okay. Remarkably enough I didn't even have a bruise on me but I also, being a kid of those days, I had no identification on me and that time I worked for a state park so I had my, and we had these sort of skivvies, I don't know what you'd call them, some type of uniform but not quite a uniform, it more looked like a prison outfit. It was a sort of gray, dingy cotton thing and I was heading to work directly so I figured I'll put it on and get there. And at any rate, this is 400 miles from home, and I was compartmentalist long enough, a state trooper arrived, I was able to tell him who I was

and what my phone number was and then I passed out. And I woke up in a hospital, a couple of days later. After having this very serene sort of experience, I actually left my body from the hospital bed and rose above the bed and was sort of in the corner by the ceiling in the wall there. And I was watching the doctors come and go and the nurses and so on and then all of a sudden I woke up and my mother was at the foot of the bed and this is just what a mother loves to hear, you know, I go, what are you doing here? Get the picture why I don't have children. But so, you know, I had this experience and it was like, God, everything is really okay. Like, it doesn't matter. And I'd been doing

TM prior to that and I'd been having these experiences in TM where it was like, I would become almost, I would feel as though I were, what, like you could put my hand through me or something. Or if I got up too soon after meditation went out, I think I could walk through the door, you know. At any rate, so I had this experience and I remember driving home and my mother obviously was upset and I remember saying to her, don't worry. And then I used this dumb phrase like, it doesn't matter. Everything is okay, you know. And she didn't particularly buy into that. But something happened, you know. And when I went back to school that next semester it became very clear to me that the interesting thing too is I then I also found

out that I stopped doing TM because I had the proclivity to sort of take off and started sitting Zen where you don't go anywhere. And yeah, and took a long time. Then, you know, I trundled out. This is February 1972. The second semester of my sophomore year was going, starting. I called my mom up and said, I'm taking a leave of absence. That's just what your mom wants to hear. I think, you know, she didn't go to college. She grew up in Brooklyn, the daughter of, the youngest daughter of eight children, an Italian immigrant, brought up mostly by her step-sister or half-sister. Apparently his father, a number of wives had died. Things like the flu and all that stuff were pretty nasty then. At any

rate, she didn't particularly appreciate that. And I couldn't particularly understand it. And I didn't exactly have the emotional space to be able to explain it to her. In any way, you know, it's all reaction. At least in the conversation with my mom. So I went out to the Zen Center, hitchhiked out, checked it out. And then I did this thing where I said, yeah, this is where I want to be. Actually, I left thinking I might go to Japan, but then I met these people who'd send me here and I went there. And then I met people at the Zen Center in San Francisco and yeah, this works and so on. So then I went back home and I told my mom what I was going to do. And then before I left

home, we took a trip together around the United States. She'd never been beyond Pennsylvania. So here I am, this 19-year-old guy with actually a beard and long hair, driving around with his mom in a Pontiac Catalina around the country, staying in holiday inns and what have you. And having a reasonably good time, being not as difficult as I might have been, I think. And then we got as far as got to San Francisco and I showed her the Zen Center and then we took a trip down to Tassajara and I showed her Tassajara because I wanted her to know that I wasn't going off to Gyan. I didn't know that yet, but go off to Gyan to take Kool-Aid or whatever. And this really made sense

considering what I was studying and these people are okay and the stuff that happens here isn't so bad. And then we drove home, the northern route, whatever. And then I came back and took up residence at the Zen Center operation. And my first job there, I used to work at Kirby's Ice Cream Polar, which is at the corner of Laguna between Fell and Oak, I think, where the old expressway used to come down. And that neighborhood is known for its poverty, prostitution, male and female, drugs, so on and so forth. And I would work at this little ice cream joint making banana, walnut ice cream or whatever and serving it. And we would close like at midnight.

So somewhere after 10 o'clock at night, the heroin addicts and the transvestites, prostressors and prostitutes would show up looking for their sweet fixes with runny noses and so on. And then also across the street, there was this wonderful blues bar that was all frequented by black people in their 1970s with clothes looked like then from whatever those movies are. And I remember going to that place one night or two nights, actually, with a woman named Peggy Regue. And Peggy was also a young Zen student who left to become a lawyer, went to Berkeley. So there we were. And then slowly I got more entrenched and more involved in the Zen center. But my aim

basically was to go there to study, to find a job that would support and pay my rent so I could work four or five hours a day and sit Zazen and basically study Buddhism. And I did that. And then, you know, shipped off to Tassajara for three years and then came back and was involved in at Green Gulch for a little while and was involved and was ordained. And Richard Baker was my teacher. And I had some incredible contact with him. Richard was the first person that I really met who I felt I could talk to. And one great thing, I think, one important thing in Buddhism is being with a teacher you can talk to, whether what you're saying means anything. But if you have the experience that you're able

to say things, are you expressing yourself? This is good. And the only way that a teacher can help us is for us to speak, to reveal ourselves to them as we reveal ourselves to ourselves. It's easily a two-way street. We have to put that energy forth. And to find someone that you can work with that allows that to occur is really great. I was fortuitous enough that in fact I met Richard and we worked together and I felt very close with him for many years. And he was able to hook me up with my next mentor who was a woman on the East Coast by the name of Nancy Wilson Ross. And Nancy is dead now. She died in 19, I want to say, 87. She was born in 1904. She comes from more or less this

neck of the woods. I think she grew up in somewhere down near Olympia. Her family came, what was her family's name? I may remember it, but they came from New England to the northwest in the mid-19th century and were involved with lumber or something. She was one of the first, she went to the University of Oregon and graduated from there like in 1920-something or other, was a bright woman. And she, amongst incredible history, she was involved in Buddhism in New York way back in the 30s with, there's a Zen teacher who was Sokayang, I think his name was. The first Zen Institute of America grew up from his and a woman named Mary Farkas established. And Nancy was deeply involved and central in helping to get Buddhism

established in western, I'll say rich people's culture, so to speak. She was on the board of the Japan Society and the Asia Society and wrote a number of books and was incredibly well-connected and helped the Zen world of the 70s actually make connections with people who had money to support it. So the Johnsons of fidelity world, John Rockefeller and Lawrence Rockefeller and remember the Chester Carlson of Xerox. These are all people who gave millions of dollars to establish Buddhism in America in the 70s and 80s and were very friendly. And they helped the Zen Center and they helped other Zen Centers. They helped I guess Edo Roshi as well. And I was lucky enough to be involved with Nancy. I helped her write her

last book, which I think is called Buddhism, A Way of Life and Thought. And as she said, this book, she would say to me and a number of us, this is for your parents so that they can get some sense of what you're doing and how you're doing it. It wasn't meant to be necessarily a Dharma book, but it was meant to be a book that could familiarize people with the culture from where it came and the things and the stories about how it was organized. When I came back to the Zen Center from Nancy's, I spent pretty much like off and on three years there in New York City, sort of Upper East Side type stuff and the North Shore of Long Island and met incredible, remarkable people. I remember

one day riding in a taxi from some party and I'm this 25 year old kid from a place called West Isla that is basically a block of split levels. And I'm in a taxi cab driving north, uptown from Greenwich Village with Franz Klein's wife and just amazing things. And getting a private tour from Blanchette Rockefeller of the Museum of Modern Art Cezanne show, it's like magic in some funny way. At any rate, when I came back to the Zen Center, I became Dick's assistant. So I was sort of like 24 hours 7 with him and worked hard and did things. At a certain point, Dick and I, it was about 1983, it was like, this is another aspect of how you relate with your teacher. It was like I couldn't talk with

him anymore. It was like, in fact, almost like he was, my experience was he was blocking me in my practice. That in fact, certain situations were happening where it didn't feel helpful to me. So I'd been at the Zen Center from 19 to 32 or so, I guess, 32, this 32 year. I thought I wanted to go off and return to the university, finish up there and go off, see what the world was about in some way. Dick didn't particularly like that idea, but it wasn't that at all that happened, really. But so then, of course, the events of 1983-84 unfolded. And at that time, I was the Eno at the city center. And so I decided to stay another year to help, if I could, stabilize things.

And I did. And then I felt very strongly that, hey, wow, it's not working with Dick anymore. And the number of people who are just senior to me, who looked like they were going to, at the time it looked like to me, sort of take control of the Zen Center, if you will, I didn't feel as though I could mature there. And I felt I needed to be someplace else to learn and study. So I left. And I went back to the university and I got some degrees. And then I went into business to pay off my debts. And then I built a division of a regional financial planning firm, from nothing to relatively a good size business. And then at a certain point, after doing that, I'm very good at sort of

zeroing in on something and then focusing on it and getting it done. That's where maverick, the term, comes in. And so I did that. And it was really great. And I was totally engrossed in it and made this thing happen. And then one day I woke up and I said, I'm in management. And I'm really a nice guy. But I have a really hard time managing to what I call the status quo. And I'm much better at starting things up and making things go and then getting the next thing going. So my partners agreed. And so I went back more into personal practice and at the same time fell in love with sailing. And then, you know, I'm dangerous. I fall in love with these things. And the next thing I knew, I was applying to be in a sailboat race

around the world. And the next thing I knew, I was accepted. And the next thing I know, I was studying weather and navigation. And I was the navigator and tactician on this team race around the world with 12 identical one design yachts in 2000, 2001. And I did that. And I came back and it was like, God, I can't be in an office. I'd been outside so much. And it was so wondrous, the idea of being in one of those offices. Not the experience, my skin crawled. But yeah, God, there's so many stories to tell. I can't tell you what it's like being out in the southern ocean. Or I can, I'll tell you this little bit. You know, the air temperature is 32 degrees, the water temperature is 32 degrees,

the wind's blowing 50 or 60 knots, and the seas are 50 feet high. And it's pitch black. And you're wet. And we only have two people on deck, one person manning the main sheet on the big mainsail to let it go in case big winds hit and one person helming. And I was one of the helming people. The main sheet person could only stay on deck for 15 minutes stints and the helms person could only helm for 30 minutes at a time. And then we'd switch. But from here to where Karen is would be the main sheet person and I'd be on the helm and I could shout at the top of my lungs. She wouldn't hear me. However, you know, you're dead dog tired and you know, you're going to get awful wet. And despite all this

high tech clothing we had, and you don't necessarily want to go out there. So feel like that sometimes. But you do. And then then what happens is the southern lights appear and the sky starts filling in with this great beige and amber light that's crawling up sort of the sides of the horizon and wiggling. And then it sort of forms this dome over you and there's green and blue and red in it. And it's going shh. You feel like you're in this incredible cathedral. It's like you forget you're freezing to death and soaking wet. And it's easy. You can't see anything and there are icebergs out there. And then then there are these things called Magellanic clouds, which are like they for all intents and premises, they appear

in the sky in the dark of the night like a white cumulus cloud. And what they are is this cloud of negatively charged ions that are just swelling and going. It's amazing. So anyway, I got back from this trip and I became a professional sailboat captain and would train people to sail boats in the ocean and sail boats from New England to the Caribbean, Caribbean to New England, across the ocean and back. And despite all this wonderful stuff, one day a friend of mine, whom I was ordained with, I think we were ordained in 1977, and David is a teacher in the Shambhala lineage now, 2003 I think it was. David called me up November and said, John, I'm going to be in town for five days. Can I stay

with you? And David and I had been remained friends since we were kids. We both arrived at the Zen Center when we were 19. We both were out there at Green Gulch breaking clods of clay with rakes and so on as volunteer labor. And then he came and he visited and we had a good time and great conversations. And then I took him up to Karma Choling in northern Vermont where he had a big meeting and met some wonderful people. And then I came back home and he had his meeting and then he went back to Germany. And then about three weeks later, he called me up and he said, John, I'm leading a program called Sutrayana Seminary at Dechen Choling in France. It's a 30-day program. Do you want to come? I said, sure. Just not even
